cim: Opinion: Artificial intelligence and technological convenience is killing the human experience
cim_eredeti: Opinion: Artificial intelligence and technological convenience is killing the human experience
szoveg_eredeti:
Last week, I walked from the Quad to the Student Union and counted eight people. Every single one of them had a phone in their hand and earbuds in their ears. Nobody said a word to anybody. We all share a campus, a mascot and a Saturday night in Tiger Stadium, but on a Tuesday afternoon we barely share a fleeting exchange.

When was the last time you had an actual conversation with a stranger? An actually in-depth conversation beyond just “I can’t believe it’s still this hot in October.” The fact that most people would have to really think about that question is a problem. We are actively losing the art of interaction.

Granted, technology doesn’t have a mission to isolate us, though it sure can feel that way. It was intended to make life easier and just happened to indirectly challenge us even more. Nowadays, I feel like it’s so hard to notice what is lost when everything is given to us on a silver platter.

You can do so much without even leaving your room. DoorDash brings dinner to your door. Instacart shops for your groceries. Amazon can deliver a charger by drone to your house within 24 hours. Tinder makes romantic suitors feel limitless with infinite swipes, judging a person based on appearance in three seconds. E-books and Kindle allow you to never even step foot inside a library.

Individually, these apps don’t seem all that bad, because really, who doesn’t want dinner delivered hot and ready to their door? But the reality of the situation is that these apps aren’t just letting us rest up after a long day by avoiding a bothersome task. They’re actively keeping us boarded up in our rooms, they’re grinding our real life, human-to-human, social capabilities into the ground.”

It seems like we have engineered away friction even though friction and growth — being curious, trying, failing, failing again maybe five more times and then finally succeeding — is the exact thing that gave us this technology in the first place.

Wandering a grocery store is a small nuisance with big social opportunities. Things as simple as running into a neighbor, asking an employee a question about a food item or taking a stranger’s suggestion on a certain seasoning have all been manufactured away through Instacart.

The same could be said for finding a book in the library and picking up two more that pique your interest along the way. These “inconveniences” are connections, and they’re still important. They force you to rely on someone else, however brief. This is how community is built.

Now, we just ask ChatGPT. We ask Claude. We ask Gemini. We ask the plethora of other AI tools on our phones: Maybe this is now our community. The robotic, people-pleasing know-it-alls designed to tell you exactly what you want to hear, whenever you need to hear it. There is no more discomfort of the unknown. It is as if we have a portable Thoth on our phones.

Struggling through a problem is what makes you actually learn about a problem. Without that, we learn next to nothing. Asking peers or a professor a question about class is how things stick. You’ll remember a face-to-face interaction with another human being; I don’t think you could say the same about an interaction with ChatGPT.

It truly makes us duller, less interested, less interesting and more numb because we have diminished the effort that makes us think.

Everything has become about speed. Get the answer fast. Get the food fast. Get everything fast, faster, fastest. Time spent on other people is not time wasted, yet we treat it that way. It is good to be inconvenienced.

College should be a time to allow yourself to make mistakes. This is one of the few stretches of life where thousands of people our age are packed into a few square miles, all open to something new. Despite being around all of these students every day, we still find ways to isolate ourselves as much as possible for the sake of convenience.

Staying connected is how we as a community get through things, together, and we just can’t do that if every way to manage that is stolen from us. How is it possible to sit in a lecture hall of 300 people and not know a single name?

Sociologists famously refer to these places we are losing as “third places,” spots that aren’t home and aren’t class, where people just show up. Maybe it’s Cherrybomb Coffee Co. right off of campus, maybe it’s the UREC or Free Speech Alley. A community can only exist if you keep showing up for it, and most of us aren’t. It’s important to show up mentally, too – not just physically. Shut your phone off and allow yourself to be a victim of oh-so-dreaded conversation

Every skipped trip to a third place is a conversation that never happened, an opportunity lost, and a friendship or relationship that never sparked. When enough of us stay in and avoid inconvenience like the plague, these places begin to lose meaning.

Personally I think we should throw all our phones into the Mississippi River or into the mini flash floods that sometimes invade LSU. Joking … unless you want to. I won’t stop you.

Really, though. Walk or drive to your go-to restaurant instead of paying $20 more for a 45-minute delivery. Leave an earbud out on the way to class. Maybe say hi to the person next to you, whether it’s in line or in class. It might be awkward, but awkwardness is the point. We need awkwardness, we need cringe, we need weird. We need people to talk.

We are only trapped by technology if we allow it.

Jeanne Warren is a 20-year-old mass communication major from Baton Rouge.
